case_study_insert.main_stem: Northbrook Nursery Group (NNG) is a cooperative in the education sector, providing early-years childcare and employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2016 by Denise North, it operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. NNG plans to invest $420,000 in two new nursery rooms and outdoor play areas, financed by $220,000 leasing and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $48, and currently produces 14,000 units a year, each a funded childcare place. NNG faces two problems: nursery assistant absenteeism has reached 10% and parent complaints about waiting lists in the new rooms are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Marketing and Quality Extract — Q3 2025: NNG filled 3,200 childcare places last quarter with a parent satisfaction rate of 88%, up from 81% a year ago. Parent complaints fell from 30 to 18 per month. Average waiting-list time is 11 days. A survey of 400 parents found that 74% would pay $10 more per week for extended hours, and 63% choose a nursery by inspection rating. Records show 11 of 38 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new safeguarding app; certification costs $550 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Northbrook Nursery Group for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.6% to 5.3%, increasing leasing costs for business equipment. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $13.10 to $13.87 per hour from April 2026. (3) Nursery equipment and food input costs rose 9.8% and government childcare funding fell 3.6%, while parental spending on childcare grew 3.9%.

questions.question_text: NNG plans to fund part of its $420,000 expansion with $220,000 leasing. Explain two advantages for NNG of using retained profit instead of leasing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit of $200,000 avoids the regular lease rentals and interest built into the $220,000 leasing deal, so NNG keeps more of the $36 contribution on each $48 childcare place. The cash saved can cover the $180,000 fixed costs and the 9.8% rise in food and equipment costs, helping the cooperative hold the price parents pay while two new rooms open.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves ownership of the new rooms and outdoor areas with the cooperative, whereas under leasing the lessor owns the assets until the term ends and may repossess them if payments lapse. Since NNG is a cooperative with 38 staff and 14,000 funded places to protect, avoiding that commitment preserves member control and adds no further interest payable beyond the $26,000 shown in Appendix 2.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to NNG's financing choice and childcare-place economics.

questions.question_text: NNG is promoting two new nursery rooms. Consider local radio advertising, parent referral incentives, or social media marketing. Which should NNG choose to fill the new places? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio advertising: Radio reaches parents in the local catchment quickly and can announce the new rooms at modest cost. Its weaknesses are that listeners are not necessarily parents of nursery-age children, it cannot show the 88% satisfaction rate, and the message disappears as soon as the advert ends, so it may not fill the places created by the $420,000 investment.

Parent referral incentives: Rewards for existing families who recommend NNG use trusted word of mouth, and with 63% of parents choosing by inspection rating a happy family is persuasive. Referrals are cheap and build loyalty, but they grow slowly and rely on the current parent base; with an 11-day waiting list, NNG needs volume fast, and unhappy families could spread complaints rather than referrals.

Social media marketing: Targeted local posts can reach parents exactly in NNG's catchment, show the 88% satisfaction rate and the 74% of 400 surveyed parents who would pay $10 more for extended hours, and be measured by enquiries. Advertising can be scaled room by room and adjusted quickly. It takes time to build trust and requires accurate, sensitive content about children, but cost per enrolled family is low.

Recommendation: NNG should choose social media marketing. It targets parents precisely, carries the satisfaction and extended-hours message and scales across two new rooms far better than radio or referrals. Local radio is rejected as untargeted and fleeting, and referral incentives are rejected as too slow while the waiting list is 11 days; NNG can add a referral bonus once the rooms are full.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited identification of the promotional options with minimal reference to NNG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some application to NNG and partial judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in NNG's context with a justified recommendation explaining why radio and referrals are rejected.

questions.question_text: NNG's nursery assistant absenteeism has reached 10% and parent complaints about waiting lists are rising. Explain two benefits for NNG of using team working to improve attendance and reduce complaints.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working lets NNG's 38 staff cover one another's shifts when absenteeism reaches 10%, so the 14,000 childcare places remain supervised rather than closing a room. Teams can share the waiting-list and safeguarding app duties, helping cut the 11-day wait and the parent complaints, and protecting the places needed to justify the $420,000 investment.

Point 2: Working in teams spreads knowledge of the new safeguarding app, so the 11 of 38 staff still untrained can learn from colleagues during normal routines rather than waiting for a course. Shared responsibility lifts the 88% parent satisfaction rate and gives assistants more involvement, which raises commitment and reduces the 10% absence rate within Denise North's hierarchical structure.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to NNG's absence, waiting list and quality data.

questions.question_text: NNG must train 11 nursery assistants on the new safeguarding app. Consider on-the-job training or certification courses at $550 per employee. Which should NNG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training during normal nursery routines teaches NNG's own safeguarding procedures, costs no fees and keeps the 11 assistants working with children while they learn, protecting the 3,200 places filled last quarter. Senior staff can mentor the 11 of 38 who are still untrained, and coaching can be fitted around the 11-day waiting list. The limitations are that trainers have less time for their own duties, habits may be copied, and there is no certificate that parents choosing by inspection rating can see.

Certification courses: At $550 per employee, certifying 11 staff costs $6,050 (11 × $550), affordable beside the $420,000 expansion. Qualified staff strengthen NNG's safeguarding reputation and support the 88% parent satisfaction rate and the 74% of 400 parents who would pay $10 more for extended hours. However, 11 of 38 staff would be away from rooms, worsening 10% absenteeism and lengthening the waiting list, and generic content may not match NNG's exact app, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: NNG should choose on-the-job training for all 11 assistants and fund one certification course for a lead practitioner. On-the-job training is cheaper, specific to NNG's procedures and avoids losing room capacity while absence is 10%; full certification is rejected because $6,050 and 11 staff off the rota would lengthen the 11-day waiting list for limited extra relevance.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited reference to NNG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods applied to NNG, including cost and disruption.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Full evaluation of both methods in NNG's context with a justified decision that rejects full external certification and explains the cost and capacity trade-off.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NNG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($48 − $12) = $180,000 ÷ $36 = 5,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 5,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $48 − $12 = $36. Answer: contribution per unit is $36.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NNG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 5,000-unit break-even output with 14,000 places actually filled: the margin of safety is 9,000 places, showing the two new rooms have a large cushion and supporting the $420,000 investment.
2. Use the $36 contribution on a $48 place to test pricing: 74% of 400 parents would pay $10 more for extended hours, so managers can weigh a premium against any fall in enrolment.
3. Check that 5,000 break-even places generate enough contribution to meet the $220,000 leasing commitment before opening more rooms.
4. Track unit cost of $24.86 per place ($180,000 ÷ 14,000 = $12.86 fixed plus $12 variable) to control 9.8% food and equipment inflation and to examine the 10% absence and 88% satisfaction rate behind the 11-day waiting list.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 5,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $36 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 9,000 against 14,000 places; pricing using the $10 extended-hours premium; meeting the $220,000 leasing commitment; and unit-cost benchmarking at $24.86.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NNG's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has NNG's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 17.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue increased from $840,000 to $1,020,000 while cost of sales rose from $504,000 to $561,000, so gross profit went from $336,000 to $459,000. Gross profit as a share of revenue therefore improved from 40.0% to 45.0%. Operating profit rose from $84,000 to $153,000, lifting operating profit as a share of revenue from 10.0% to 15.0%. Capital employed increased from $700,000 to $900,000, giving a return on capital of 12.0% in 2024 and 17.0% in 2025.

Evaluation: All three measures improved, and the strongest gain is in operating profit as a share of revenue, suggesting fixed costs of $180,000 are being spread over more childcare places as the cooperative grew. The share of revenue left after direct costs also rose, showing control of food and staffing costs despite 9.8% input inflation. However, interest payable rose from $18,000 to $26,000 as leasing took effect, and capital employed grew by $200,000 while operating profit grew by $69,000, so return on capital improved well. The 10% absence and 11-day waiting list could still damage satisfaction, and the extract gives no breakdown of government childcare funding.

Conclusion: NNG's financial performance has improved. Gross profit as a share of revenue rose from 40.0% to 45.0%, operating profit as a share of revenue from 10.0% to 15.0%, and return on capital from 12.0% to 17.0%. All three measures rise together and the largest gain is in operating return, so the improvement is solid, though higher leasing costs and the waiting list mean management must protect service quality.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or directional changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs and capital employed and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NNG of offering extended opening hours at the new nursery rooms.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Extended hours meet a clear parent need. NNG's survey found 74% of 400 parents would pay $10 more per week for extended hours and 63% choose a nursery by inspection rating, so a weekly premium can lift revenue above the $48 price per place and protect the $36 contribution while 9.8% costs rise. It also strengthens the case for the $420,000 rooms and play areas.

Disadvantage: Longer opening needs more staff hours, which could raise the $12 variable cost per place or push fixed costs above $180,000. With nursery assistant absenteeism at 10% and 11 of 38 staff untrained on the safeguarding app, NNG may struggle to supervise the extended sessions safely, lengthening the 11-day waiting list and risking the 88% satisfaction rate.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to NNG's survey, costs and staffing.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.3%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in nursery equipment and food costs will affect NNG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate rise (4.6% to 5.3%): Leasing costs on the new rooms are likely to be sensitive to rates. If the $220,000 leasing agreement tracks the base rate, the 0.7 percentage-point rise adds 0.7% × $220,000 = $1,540 a year at most. That is small beside $180,000 of fixed costs, and a lease fixed at the outset would mean no extra charge. Higher rates may also squeeze household budgets, but the direct cash effect on NNG is modest.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $13.87 an hour): NNG employs a workforce of 38 and assistant roles are commonly hourly-paid, so this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay rates, so an honest annual total cannot be calculated. The defensible check is productivity: 14,000 childcare places across 38 staff is about 368.4 places per employee, so the rise is absorbable only if that productivity holds; otherwise unit labour cost raises the $24.86 unit cost and narrows the $36 contribution per place.

Equipment and food cost inflation (9.8%): The $12 variable cost per place is not decomposed in the insert, so only a labelled illustrative upper bound is defensible. If the whole $12 were exposed, 9.8% × $12 = $1.18 extra per place (to 2dp), and across 14,000 places that is about $16,464 a year (14,000 × $1.176), cutting contribution from $36 toward $34.82. NNG can recover part of this through the $10 extended-hours premium that 74% of surveyed parents accept, though the 3.6% funding cut limits help from government.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in equipment and food costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 14,000 places and directly erodes the $36 contribution that supports the $420,000 expansion, and a leasing decision cannot remove it. The wage rise is second but cannot be quantified from the insert, while the rate rise adds at most $1,540 a year and is clearly the smallest of the three changes.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to NNG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on NNG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in NNG's context with a justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
